maintopic: GOOD WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: It is a pleasure for me on behalf of this party to offer our very best wishes to the Prime Minister on this, his birthday. I suppose many of us remember the day more specifically because it is St. George's day, when goodness traditionally triumphed over evil.

maintopic: GOOD WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our group I should like to extend to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) our best wishes on the occasion of his birthday.
I want to take this opportunity to underline the important achievements of the Prime Minister as far as recognition of the groups which make up our country is concerned. Never in the history of Canada, in my opinion, has a Prime Minister so efficiently and effectively taken a stand on the recognition of the two main ethnic groups of our country, the French Canadians and the English Canadians.
Our opinion may differ from that of the Prime Minister on many occasions, Mr. Speaker, but that does not prevent us from seeing in him a great Canadian. I hope he will be with us for a long time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: GOOD WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER ON BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
I should like very sincerely to acknowledge with gratitude the kind words of the Leader of the Opposition and the leaders of the other parties. Those words remind us that there are personal friendships and personal good will which know no party boundaries. I am, as I believe each of us is, a beneficiary of this spirit of parliament. Political life is difficult, but it would be infinitely more difficult if we did not have these amenities, and I am grateful for the kind words which have been said to me on my birthday. But, Mr. Speaker,
I confess that the last birthday seems an awfully long time back.

Mr. Speaker, under standing order 26 I move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the extension of the winter works program in designated areas.
Mr. Speaker, standing order 26 states that in order to move the adjournment of the house, a definite matter of urgent public importance must be involved. The matter I wish to have discussed today is extremely definite and restricted, namely the extension of the winter works program in designated areas.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in his budget speech, which is the most important speech of the year, stated-

speechtext:
The Minister of Finance stated in his budget speech-that is the most important speech-as reported in Hansard, at page 970, left hand column:
Our first goal is high level employment.
And at page 972, left hand column, at the top of the page:
Our plans and policies are designed to meet the special needs of areas of the country or groups of the population confronted with special difficulties and problems.
The situation itself proves that the matter is important, since the Minister of Finance

himself recognizes that this is the primary objective of the Canadian government, and duty of the opposition is to help the government achieve this objective.
Third, the matter is national in scope and of general interest, since it concerns 35 designated areas and will also help to balance the situation for the areas and for the people, along the lines advocated by the Prime Minister and the present government, who have always hoped for it and who have devoted their energies toward a greater unity and a better national understanding. In addition, that will put an end to the discrimination that prevails in various regions of the country because weather conditions differ. The most beautiful regions, with the best weather conditions have the highest employment rate, whereas the regions where the weather conditions are harsher in winter have the highest unemployment rate. Those are the regions where unemployment is most severe and they are precisely the areas designated by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen).
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, it is a very urgent matter since today is the 23rd of April and the winter works period is supposed to end on April 30, which means that there are only seven days left to solve that problem.
Furthermore, we will have no other opportunity to discuss the matter prior to April 30, and after that date it will be too late.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that this motion meets all the requirements of standing order 26, for it deals with a definite matter, the most important we have to discuss. Furthermore, and the Minister of Finance admitted it in his budget speech, it is of general interest, national in scope and extremely urgent, since the winter works period will expire soon and we will have no other opportunity of discussing this matter.
This motion also meets all the requirements of paragraph 6 of standing order 26. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), that the proceedings of the house be adjourned in order to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the extension of the winter works period beyond April 30 in designated areas.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 22, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-72, to provide for the establishment of electoral boundaries commissions to report upon the readjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons and to provide for the readjustment of such representation in accordance therewith-Mr. Pickersgill (for Mr. Pearson)-Mr. Lamou-reux in the chair.
On clause 6-Appointment of chairman, etc.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Yesterday, when the committee rose, I was pointing out that redistribution has definite political results and that no one can prevent such results occurring.
Since Governor Elbridge Gerry became famous for it some 150 years ago, the only real danger in redistribution has been the danger of favouritism toward the government in power. I think that so-called gerrymandering over the years has always been the case of a government in power facing accusations, often well founded, of adjusting the boundaries of a riding for its own benefit. I think the danger we have to face is this danger, and I believe that is why the government in the present bill has attempted, as did the previous government in the course of a somewhat similar proposal, to remove the question of redistribution from politics.
I ask why it is that having proposed a method of appointing commissioners which seemed fair at the time, and which was acceptable to the official opposition, the government should now favour another method. Is it simply because the official opposition favours it, or is it because the government has discovered an advantage in the new proposal? With all due credit to the Minister of Transport, who accepts paternity for drawing up this bill, I do not believe he would have drawn up one of the most basic clauses in this measure without consulting with the Prime Minister and his colleagues. I ask him-and this is a rhetorical question-why the change? It certainly is enough to make an opposition party very suspicious.
The object of the bill is to have a fair and equitable redistribution without favouring the government party. Furthermore, we want to accomplish this political task, which parliament apparently finds too difficult to handle
2492	HOUSE OF
Electoral Boundaries Commission itself, without leaving the smear of partisanship on those who do it. This is the whole point of my argument today, and this is the whole reason I support the original draft. I hope I can express my reasons clearly.
Every boundary change has political results due to traditional voting patterns. To say otherwise, of course, is incorrect. This is more than merely changing the geography; it is political. It is just so much nonsense to say that the commission can be or ought to be insensitive to the political results of their decisions. In my view the whole point is that they must not be insensitive to the results of their decisions.
If the commissions were given clear directions, a precise formula or tolerance they were bound to follow in changing riding boundaries, perhaps they could operate within this pure vacuum of a mathematical or similar formula that we might create for them. We do not give them this formula, and I do not know how we could. We give them very broad directions that they are to take into account geographical locations and so forth. They will have to do the best they can, and they have an outside tolerance beyond which they should not go. How can they avoid trouble? I do not believe they can. The very first thing that a commission has to decide, for example, is how many seats the province they are concerned with is entitled to under the British North America Act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: They do not decide that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: The Minister of Transport says they do not decide that. I should like to know who does.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will read the act passed at the last session of parliament he will see it is set out right in that act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot accept that statement, because the B.N.A. Act is capable of interpretation in several ways. I am advised that one or two cases it is capable of different interpretations. However, I am not making this a point. I am just saying this is an example. Suppose the commissions in each of the 10 provinces decide on a somewhat different basis as to what should be the total number of seats in the particular province. Where are we then? I think this is a difficulty, but it is not the main difficulty on which I base my argument.
It is logical that we must do three things. First, we must remove any lingering suspicion that the fine hand of the government is behind decisions on boundaries. We must remove this suspicion regardless of whether or not any such fine hand is involved. Second, 

we must remove any suspicion that the commissions will be mere rubber stamps for plans prepared under government supervision or at least under supervision of an official. We must remove suspicion that there will be a closed door behind which these commissions will work, and we should require that a member be admitted who is adverse to the interests of the government with respect to redistribution in order to see what is going on in these commissions.
I am not raising any question about the propriety of the actions these commissions will take. I know they will start out to do a good job. But we must not only see that redistribution is fair; it must appear to be fair, and it must be accepted as such or we will put these public officials, particularly the judges, in a difficult position.
I should like to look for a moment at the two proposals before us regarding the composition of the commissions. In both cases the chairman will be a superior court judge and the second member will be the representation commissioner. With this I entirely agree, but I ask this question. Why do we all agree on the choice of a judge? The answer is that judges are accustomed to hearing evidence and coming to a logical and fair conclusion after hearing the various views. Second, we favour a judge because he, being appointed for life, has no political interest to serve. He is able and trained to act without fear or favour in the result. But how can a judge decide without having opposing views to consider or any views to consider?
The representation commissioner, like the judge, is going to be objective and impartial. This has to be his job. Is it up to the representation commissioner to point out to the judge chairing the commission the political consequences of every riding change and the political consequences of the whole plan? Surely this is not the job of the representation commissioner. He is not political, and surely it should not be the representation commissioner who should go to the chairman of the commission and say "If you move this one over, there is a big group of Conservatives there and they will benefit; or if you move that line farther north there is a group of Liberals there who will benefit". Surely this is not the job of the representation commissioner. Certainly it is not the job of the judge.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Or of anybody else.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
He is supposed to be impartial and I am sure he will be. So I say that the representation commissioner cannot put forward any political views to the commission. The Minister of Transport has just said that

nobody should consider the political consequences of these changes. I agree with him that nobody should, but it is impossible to do this job without considering the political consequences. It is impossible to do so. They are tied as closely to the job of redistribution as the peel is to the orange, and cannot be separated from it. That is why we are divesting ourselves of the job. Anybody with a mathematical mind could draw lines on a map. Anybody with a mathematical mind could take the riding boundaries and say "We will take a little off here and make the riding square; it will look better square". This would be the result. Therefore we cannot accept that no politics are involved. We cannot accept that redistribution must be done in a vacuum. We are giving the job to a judge, the representation commissioner and two other people. When we give it to them we expect them to consider the facts and they have got to consider the political consequences.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would permit a question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman saying that the other two commissioners should not be just as non-partisan and independent as the judge and the representation commissioner?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am saying that one of them must represent a political viewpoint opposed to that of the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: May I finish this point. I hear a great chorus of objections. I cannot believe and I do not know of anyone here who can believe that this job can be done in a vacuum, who can say that political consequences have nothing to do with the matter and they must not be considered. The commissioners are going to be made aware of the political factor surreptitiously. Let us be honest about it. Somebody is going to whisper. The judge, the representation commissioner and the other two members are going to wonder about it themselves. They are going to wonder what the result is going to be of changing a boundary. They will say to themselves "Somebody has told us it would be a good idea to move this boundary this way. Now, we know it is going to take in 1,000 more people and it is going to bring that constituency up to the limit. What is the result going to be? Will it scuttle a Conservative member or a Liberal member?"

speechtext: It is impossible to deal with it otherwise.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question?

speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: The Conservative government of Ontario has established a commission, which is in existence now, consisting of a high court judge, the chief electoral officer of that province and a professor from Queen's University. It was established under the aegis of Mr. Frost who I thought, at one time, was rather admired over there. I should like to ask the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka which one of these three commissioners represented the Tories and which one represented the Liberals, if I follow his argument correctly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
The answer is none. There is quite a difference between provincial redistribution and federal redistribution. Let us not be naive, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps the hon. member who is asking all the questions is one of the principal reasons we are concerned.
I come to another point, and that is the method of appointment of the two other commissioners. We have a judge and the representation commissioner. Under the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the judge appoints the other two from a specific group of persons. Now, what is the judge supposed to do? Is he supposed to pick members with different political views? Is he supposed to pick one with a right wing view and one with a left wing view? I do not believe this is his job. He is not supposed to know. He is not supposed to be concerned with the political views of the other commissioners.
Is he supposed to pick members with no political views? If you can find a university person who is interested in redistribution and who has no political views or political ties, I will be very surprised. You cannot find them. If they are at all interested in politics, then they have views and we have heard many of them on radio and television. They are the greatest proponents of political views, and I have no objection to this. If people with no political views were appointed to serve with the judge, what help would they be in assisting him in deciding upon the political consequences of redistribution on an individual riding or on the whole plan? They would be of no help to him, if such people could be found.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, the answer is to have the leaders of the two principal parties in the house nominate people who could represent the opposing political views. I refuse to believe that this is not the reason
2494	HOUSE OF
Electoral Boundaries Commission we have an impartial member on the commission, an impartial judge as chairman. If there is a division, two and two, what is the impartial chairman there for if not to make the decision? However, he has to be told what the political consequences are. I am sure of this. I do not believe anyone would suggest they could operate in a vacuum. If the commissioners do not know, they will find out. For example, are they going to blindly cast a map of the province of Ontario favouring the Liberal party all across the board? I would not think so. I do not think they would do that if they knew. Are they going to cast a map rewriting the boundaries favouring the Conservative party, the New Democrats or the Social Credit party in Ontario, purposely giving them an advantage? I do not think so.
I believe the desire is that the members have the whole picture, have all the facts and know what they are doing before they redraw the electoral boundaries of the provinces concerned. They must know all the facts. They must have the political facts openly. There must be members on the commission who will open the door and prevent secrecy. As I said in the beginning, this suspicion must be removed that there is a behind the doors transaction, that there is a closed door deal and that nobody can look into it. We must remove the suspicion that no one will know exactly what is happening until the plans are laid on the table of the House of Commons. At that time we know it is valueless to object because the house has no authority to change those plans. I personally do not agree with that particular provision in the bill, but I am prepared to accept it. We have no power to change the plan here.
I say therefore, Mr. Chairman, that the best proposition for handling this gigantic job across Canada is to have two political persons, not political figures but political appointments to the commission. I want to echo what was said by the hon. member for Edmonton West yesterday. I do not believe, myself, that being a politician is anything very terrible. I do not believe that the Prime Minister of Canada and the Leader of the Opposition cannot make reasonable and fair nominations for this job. I do not believe there is any question but that these nominations could be made openly and aboveboard, so that everyone could see. Do not hide politics under the rug.

gentleman would permit me to ask one question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

I want to deal with this nonsensical argument about university professors. I do not know where hon. members have got their information that somehow the university professors of this country are all lined up in political camps, and you can press a button and so many will line up in each individual camp. I have taken a particular interest in this and I would say to hon. members who put forward this argument that knowing university faculties as I do, you could not identify on any university, by any kind of political activity of a partisan nature, more than 25 per cent of the professors.
I am quite willing to concede that very few of those who are out in the open are Conservative party supporters, but that happens to be occasioned by something completely different, something inherent in the philosophies and attitudes of that party. To get up and suggest that the university professors of this country are a partisan group is nonsensical. I know the hon. member for Carleton could possibly say a lot on this subject.
I can remember speaking to a group of professors at Carleton University a few years ago, when all the professors were gathered together, and at this particular consultation I made the argument, which was supported by one other hon. member of the house, that university professors should take a more active part in party politics, but the response of the meeting was overwhelmingly against that. Repeatedly the professors got up and said they would much sooner deal directly with civil servants than with politicians. Therefore this particular argument that university professors are politically partisan is silly. One can go to Queen's University and look at the social science faculties there. Aside from four or five people, I think you would find some 25 have no connection with any political party and have never taken part in partisan activity. It is a nonsense argument.
Electoral Boundaries Commission
Now I want to touch on another phase of this argument. We are concerned in any kind or manner of redistribution with what the Americans call malapportionment. We want to get one vote equalling another vote in another part of the country, and the traditional fear of politicians is gerrymandering when redistribution takes place. That is the thing about which I am so much worried. I want to give a hypothetical case in connection with the constituency of Port Arthur. It is going to be chopped severely in the coming redistribution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: How do you know until the commission is set up? Would you answer that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Yes, I can answer that question because we are away above the median in terms of population, even if we have a 30 per cent tolerance, so obviously the constituency is going to be altered. On one side there is Fort William, and adjacent to Fort William there is a section of the constituency that traditionally has voted overwhelmingly C.C.F. or N.D.P. Down at the other end of the constituency there is a section which has traditionally more overwhelmingly voted Liberal, and in another corner there is an area that has consistently voted Conservative.
The obvious fear in all members' minds is about what redistribution will do. I would rather put it into an area wherein it would be handled by other than members of the House of Commons.
With this happy thought I read Bill No. C-72 when it was first drafted, and on reading the clauses in that bill I must say that I felt it was very fair; so much so that I could not see much wrong with the bill except for one point, and that was with regard to the provision of tolerance. The reason I took exception to that matter and thought it should be higher in percentage points was because I felt that the low percentage points of tolerance would create a parochial type of member of parliament.
At the moment we have members of parliament who represent urban constituencies and portions of agricultural areas. As a result they have a broader view and feel inclined as a matter of responsibility to take into consideration the agricultural side of life in Canada as well as the urban side. A smaller tolerance would have a tendency to create, as I say, parochial members of parliament in that a member will be representing an urban area only while another will be representing an agricultural area only. I am taking exception to this and I hope that when we reach this clause the government will see the light and see fit to make some adjustments in this connection.

I ran for parliament on a political platform representing a political party and I believe my duty in the House of Commons as a member of the opposition is to provide an alternative to the present government. That is the way in which to conduct the business of this house. Too many people say we should be non-partisan here and that we should all work for the good of the country. We are all working for the good of the country. I had experience, during the setting up of a committee this morning, of the lip service that is given to non-partisanship. A chairman was elected from the government side, as is right, and after election he proceeded to thank the committee and to express the hope that the committee would carry on its work in a nonpartisan way for the good of Canada. Very good. Then the name of the vice-chairman came up for nomination, and he was a member from the Liberal side, too. That is a good example of a non-partisan attitude. They say: Let us be non-partisan but we are all going to be Liberals on this committee.
Today we have writers who are naive enough to suggest that there should be no partisanship even in the House of Commons. What are they proposing-a one party system which would eventually end in a dictatorship? No. Parliament is a place of politics and partisanship. We have a tendency, in paying lip service to the non-partisan idea, to create the same atmosphere outside, and people then look on parliament as an institution which has downgraded itself. Well, parliament is not downgraded. It is the same now as it was in 1952 when I came here. There was partisanship and politics then. That is the way I like it. That is the way it should be. That is why the democratic system works, and when we end this system we will be on the road to dictatorship in this country.

speechtext:

He said: Mr. Speaker, I shall endeavour to show the house that this request for papers is a fair and legitimate one despite the point made by the President of the Privy Council a week ago yesterday, when he invoked section 55 of the Succession Duties Act to indicate that this required secrecy. I wanted first of all, Mr. Speaker, in order to put this matter in context, to put on the record a letter I received from the minister's office on April 17, 1964. It is not marked "Personal and confidential" and I know the minister will not mind my putting it on the record:
Dear Mr. Fisher:
Mr. Mcllraith has asked me to bring to your attention the following information regarding the Eaton-Kaye estate, further to his conversation with you of yesterday.
Representations were made by Mr. Cyrus Eaton to the successive ministers of national revenue in an attempt to enlist their support and the active support of the Canadian government in resisting the claim for income tax registered against him personally by the United States tax authorities. The successive ministers-
I suppose he is here referring to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) and the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming):
-were sympathetic to Mr. Eaton but it was concluded that the Canadian government could not interfere in the action taken by the United States tax authorities applying the United States income tax law to a citizen and resident of the United States. The tax conventions were not applicable in these circumstances.
Being vested with the responsibility of collecting the taxes imposed by the Dominion Succession Duty Act. the taxation divison could no longer permit the postponement of the payment of the duties owed in connection with this estate when

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to make the point that if you look at the notice of motion it says:
*-a copy of all correspondence exchanged between the Department of National Revenue and the American authorities under the tax agreement between Canada and the United States with regard to the Eaton-Kaye case and any opinions which may have been obtained from the American authorities on the position of the securities and investment involved in the estate of the late Mrs. Eaton-Kaye since January 1, 1961.
My first point is that I am requesting the information and exchange of correspondence that has taken place between the Canadian government, particularly a department of the Canadian government, and the United States authorities in connection with this matter, and this letter that I read into the record indicates that indeed some kind of exchange almost certainly did take place, because the letter says:
The successive ministers were sympathetic to Mr. Eaton but it was concluded that the Canadian government could not interfere in the action taken by the United States tax authorities applying the United States income tax law-
Then the letter says that the tax conventions were not applicable in the circumstances. Daley, from June 1, 1958.

Mr. Cyrus Eaton is well known to most Canadians. He is one of our more famed expatriates and is well known as a patron and sponsor of the Pugwash park commission and the whole idea of the Pugwash conferences. Mrs. Eaton-Kaye was his sister and, as the point is made in the letter which I put on the record, she died some years ago. In her bequeathing, as I understand it, she made a pledge of some $100,000 to the Pugwash park commission and some $35,000 to McGill University. Obviously when someone dies that many years ago the action in so far as the succession duties is concerned drags out over this period of years, there has been a view within the Department of National Revenue that it is prepared to accept the contention of the executor of the estate, Mr. Cyrus Eaton. Then the question arises as to why in the fall of last year this contention, whatever it was, was changed or altered. Of course, it was this change that brought me to place on the order paper my motion for the production of papers, in order to get this situation opened up so that I could understand it.
I have had representations from Mr. Eaton, as I know other members of this house have. I make no bones about the fact that I have always been an admirer of Mr. Eaton, not least for his courage in expressing in the United States some views on world and international affairs that cannot help but bring him a certain kind of unpopularity and yet reflect a certain courage in outlook. I wanted to indicate, in order to put the situation as fairly as possible to the minister, that the executor in this case, Mr. Eaton, made an offer in writing last October, as I understand it, and it was made before that either orally or in writing by his solicitor. He made this offer to the department that he was prepared to provide government securities or any other

type of security that would be required or asked for by the Department of National Revenue and was prepared to put these, I think the technical term is "in escrow", or in some kind of place where they would be a perfect cover, including interest, for the obligations in connection with the estate, if the government would be prepared to delay action on the particular succession duties until this case in the United States was cleared up.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE WITH U.S. ON EATON-KAYE CASE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a point of order. The matter before the house is the motion for the production of certain papers. What the hon. member is now discussing is the detail of some tax matters of a particular individual, who happens to be involved indirectly in the case for which he is asking for papers. The hon. member is discussing the merits of that tax position, and the two matters are not related at all. What is at issue now and what should be debated is the question of whether the papers indicated in the notice of motion on the order paper should be produced. The wider question as to the merit of Mr. Eaton's philanthropies or lack of philanthropies, or the question of certain gifts which he has given or is proposing to give, is surely irrelevant to the point.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE WITH U.S. ON EATON-KAYE CASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not trying to gild the lily: I just wanted to identify the matter and I will give the minister an undertaking that I will not go off on to any other point of that kind. However, I do want an opportunity of presenting the reason why I am interested in this case and the information I request.
According to the information which I have from the executor, the largest holding in the estate is a block of Investors Trust Limited common stock. When the U.S. internal revenue service made known its intention to attempt to establish Mrs. Eaton-Kaye's brother, Cyrus Eaton, a Canadian-born American citizen, as the owner of these shares, the problem of double taxation by Canada and the United States [DOT] arose. The argument, Mr. Speaker, is simply this. If the shares which are supposedly in this estate belonged to Mr. Eaton and they are being taxed by United States authorities, obviously the question arises as to double taxation or even as to the ownership or validity of the shares which are held in the Eaton-Kaye estate.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, then minister of national revenue, thereupon agreed that Canada would withhold collection of succession duties on the Eaton-Kaye estate until the conflicting legal question between Canada and the United States could be resolved. The hon. member for Victoria- Carleton (Mr. Flemming), when he succeeded to the office of minister, naturally honoured the agreement that had been made by

his predecessor, and also undertook to initiate a conference between the appropriate Canadian and American tax authorities as provided by the tax treaty between the two countries.
Subsequently, in 1963, the Department of National Revenue instituted proceedings in the probate court in Halifax to force settlement of the estate and, failing that, to remove Cyrus Eaton as executor. A hearing in the probate court is scheduled for April 24, 1964. Meanwhile the United States internal revenue service is in full swing in its attack on Investors Trust Limited with the intention not only of collecting taxes from Cyrus Eaton on the shares owned by his late sister, but also from American minority shareholders not in any way related to the Eaton family. The minority shareholder phase is in an advanced stage in the United States tax court in Indianapolis, Indiana, in a case involving the Irwin Miller family, prominent Indianians whose principal interests are with two companies, both with important operations in Canada. The Miller case raises questions of violation of both the United States constitution and the Canadian-American tax treaty.
For the purposes of the Miller case, the United States internal revenue service temporarily bypasses its attempt to establish Cyrus Eaton as the owner of Mrs. Eaton-Kaye's Investors Trust shares, and tries to develop a new interpretation of "attribution". Even if majority ownership of Investors Trust was lodged in the late Mrs. Eaton-Kaye and her sister Mrs. Eva R. Webb, a Canadian citizen and resident, the internal revenue service contends that because their brother is an American citizen and resident, Investors Trust becomes a foreign personal holding company under American tax law, and unrelated American minority stockholders are therefore to be subjected to punitive taxation on undistributed earnings and capital gains of Investors Trust, in addition to customary taxation on dividends actually received.
Counsel for the Millers has pointed out that, if this "unreasonable, unjust and absurd" contention should be sustained, every United States citizen who happens to have made an investment in a foreign corporation that is controlled by foreign citizens with United States relatives will nevertheless be subjected to taxation upon undistributed earnings of the foreign corporation, even though the United States citizens who are subjected to the tax would have no control whatsoever over the distribution of such earnings. foreign owners had relatives who were citizens or residents of the United States. It would follow that any United States citizen investing in a bona fide Canadian enterprise would do so at great peril, and this would undoubtedly go a long way toward foreclosing American investment in Canadian enterprises.
This highlights the fact that there is a case before the United States courts brought by the United States internal revenue service dealing with this whole question of the ownership, control and status of this holding company, Investors Trust Limited. As I understand it, the contention of Mr. Eaton, the executor of the estate of Mrs. Eaton-Kaye which falls within the ambit of the Department of National Revenue, is that he has offered to cover the amount which will be levied against the estate if it stands until the time that the United States court case is settled. When the United States case is settled and the whole question of ownership is cleared up, then Eaton is prepared to proceed on the whole matter with the Department of National Revenue, and as an example of his good faith is prepared to cover the obligation which has been assigned by the Department of National Revenue.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in asking for the information contained in this motion I am asking for something that is relevant to this whole question of the tax agreement between Canada and the United States. This is not a simple, clearcut matter of succession duties or of something under the Succession Duty Act. Something much larger is involved. In my previous experience as a member of this house I have been able to obtain information from the interchange of information between the Canadian and United States tax authorities. It is only fair to put fairly bluntly the reasons why I think this information is relevant to me and other members who may be interested.
It seems to me unusual that a person having died some six years ago and some kind of arrangement-I do not know how definite or how tentative it was-is made, in light of what was developing in the United States whereby the case would not be proceeded with, and then suddenly last year, while the case was still going forward, and an offer being made to cover the amount of tax which has been levied and to place it in the form of a bond, or an escrow, or whatever the term is, that this was not accepted or taken up by the government.
I realize that it is not the real purpose of debate on motions such as this to ask the minister for a whole range of answers to everything in connection with such a complicated matter, but the reason I wish to persist with my motion and to ask for this

Motions for Papers
information is because I think that if someone Who does business in this country and is executor for an estate which affects a couple of institutions in this country of a very worthwhile kind has made some kind of request, which is usually honoured or agreed to, and has been turned down, and the government is proceeding with its action despite these representations or the previous consideration which had been given, then the government should be called upon to explain.
I know there are one or two other members in the house who wish to make some comments on this matter, and I see that I have exhausted my time, but I would plead with the minister to give us this information, and if he cannot to explain, in view of the information he has given me in this letter, why the particular material for which I ask would not be relevant to section 55 of the Succession Duty Act.

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE WITH U.S. ON EATON-KAYE CASE
speechtext:
I
rather regret we have reached this point in debate on this question because I feel that had the government been willing to co-operate with Mr. Eaton in the proposals he has made about this matter-a very serious matter for my constituents in particular- we would not be forced into this debate and into the difficult decision which the government must make when involved in personal taxation and the divulgence of information associated with it.
At the same time, when I read the notice of motion proposed by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) I find that it would be quite possible for the government to provide the type of information he desires without at the same time divulging any personal details about the tax position of the individual concerned. What the hon. member for Port Arthur appears to be concerned with is what happened all of a sudden between the government of Canada and the government of the United States in relation to this subject. For many years there had been an indication of co-operation between the Department of National Revenue in Canada and the bureau of internal revenue in the United States. One of the results of action taken in both Canada and the United States in connection with the Eaton estate is that very large sums of money presently in the estate will be swallowed up by legal fees and costs.
In this regard I should like to put on record a few comments from the chairman of the Pugwash park commission who informed me in a letter dated November 4, 1963, as follows:
As presently constituted, the park commission is playing an important part in local development, much of the money being channelled toward

educational endeavours, and I know that this sum, if made available, would be of tremendous value locally. We are fearful that the estate may be absorbed by the tax collectors in Ottawa and Washington.
I can well appreciate the concern of the Pugwash park commission in this regard. There is $100,000 involved here which would go to this commission, and though the estate is substantially larger than that, succession duties, which, I understand amount to about $111,000 on a $356,000 estate, will make considerable inroads on this money. Associated with this we must face the fact that there is no way of knowing what the net result of the court action in the United States is likely to be or what amounts the revenue bureau of the United States intends to demand. In addition, there are the court costs and the legal fees involved as a result of actions taken in the courts in the United States and in Canada.
I feel that the proposal put forward by Mr. Eaton that he would, in effect, guarantee the succession duties involved to the Canadian government if it did transpire that the Canadian government was entitled to them was one which should have been given very serious consideration. Indeed, I believe it should have been acted upon by the present government when the proposal was made. It seems to me that the correspondence which the hon. member for Port Arthur desired might well provide us with the information we need in this regard. Unless we are given access to this correspondence we are obliged to make an assumption of some sort-an assumption which comes to my mind and which I should like to have removed. That is, it may well be, if one goes back a short time in history to the Premium Iron Ore case and the many developments related to it, that officials in the Department of National Revenue in Canada and their counterparts in the United States might well have reached the point of persecuting this man because he was successful in proving that the contentions he made in the Premium Iron Ore case were correct. Here again we see this man being badgered by tax collectors both in Canada and in the United States, and should it develop that once again the position he takes is proven to be correct, then indeed the type of motion which the hon. member has brought forward will bring the facts to light and provide us with information by which we can judge what action should be taken in this regard.
As I say, I regret we have to reach the point at which the government must undertake some soul searching as to whether or not certain information should be made public. At the same time, the hon. member for Port Arthur has indicated that a former

minister of national revenue, now the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) was willing to set a precedent in this respect and make information available to the public in the Premium Iron Ore case. I hope the government will take the same attitude in this case and make available the information which is now requested, or at least that portion of the information desired which will in no way involve the personal aspect of an individual's tax submissions.
I do not know what more I can say to the Acting Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Mcllraith). I hope he will agree to the request of the hon. member for Port Arthur and try to do something which will eliminate the very heavy legal burden which is now being imposed on this estate. I should like to reiterate what the hon. member for Port Arthur has said about the man who is involved in this matter. Although he is presently a citizen of the United States, Cyrus Eaton, as I think the minister is aware, has a close association with Canada and especially with my constituency and with the village of Pugwash.
His efforts, while debatable in the minds of many, have been very significant from an international peace keeping point of view. The attention he has brought to Nova Scotia through the Pugwash conferences and his interest in agriculture in our province has been most significant. As the minister is considering this matter I hope he will consider it from the point of view of Mr. Eaton not being a citizen of the United States alone but rather a citizen of the world, a particular type of individual who has made a most significant contribution to the present state of world peace and an individual who has been very generous in his efforts to promote peace and an interest in Pugwash that will be lasting and of value to the people of my constituency.
We have a high regard for Cyrus Eaton in Cumberland county. We do not take kindly to the fact that while a former government agreed to co-operate with him to bring about the least amount of damage possible this estate is now faced with the particularly heavy burden of a lawsuit in the Canadian courts that does not need to be there. It would not be there if the government had been willing to go along with the proposal made by Mr. Eaton, but it is there because of some reason about which we have not been informed.
We would like to know why the government is taking this action. If the request for information that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) has made will provide this knowledge then I as a member of parliament am most anxious to see the informa-20220- 160i

tion tabled. I am pleased that the hon. member for Port Arthur has brought this motion forward, although I regret that it was necessary for him to have to do so. I also appreciate the problem that the minister faces in reaching a decision whether or not this information should be made public. But I must indicate to him that in view of the surrounding circumstances I have no alternative but to support the hon. member for Port Arthur in his efforts to have this information tabled and I hope the minister will also support the hon. member in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a few comments to make on this motion and they are brought about because of the fact that I had some connection with the Department of National Revenue at a time when the gentleman who is indirectly referred to in the motion had some difficulty, with which I became familiar. At that time, and in view of the circumstances which he related to me, I had no hesitation whatsoever in carrying out the suggestion made to my predecessor that the Canadian tax authorities might very properly use their influence with the American authorities with a view to implementing the very thing for which tax conventions are supposed to provide, the avoidance of double taxation. So the opinion which I expressed to the officials of the department was that an effort should be made to settle the matter with their American counterparts so that it might be settled once and for all.
I was assured by Dr. Eaton that as far as the succession duties owing to Canada were concerned they would be absolutely guaranteed, and it was on that basis that I became convinced that we should use our good offices to bring about a settlement of this matter.
With regard to the production of papers, I have some quite strong views on the production of papers relating to taxation with respect to an individual and as between countries. I think that such correspondence should be very carefully guarded. At the same time I suggest to the minister that I believe he should use his influence with the American authorities to bring about a settlement so as to avoid double taxation. I think it is possible to get this matter settled.
It is unfortunate that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) had to bring the matter before the house. I think it should have been settled without a motion for papers being necessary, but it has not been settled. I cannot vote for the production of such papers but I strongly urge the minister to use his influence and the good offices of his

Mr. Speaker, I must say 1 am somewhat surprised at the tenor of the discussion on this motion. I want to read the motion before the house. It is in these words:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this house a copy of all correspondence exchanged between the Department of National Revenue and the American authorities under the tax agreement between Canada and the United States with regard to the Eaton-Kaye case and any opinions which may have been obtained from the American authorities on the position of the securities and investment involved in the estate of the late Mrs. Eaton-Kaye since January 1, 1961.
It will be seen that the motion is so drafted as to ask for information with relation to a particular tax return, and is specifically limited to a particular tax return and the information in connection therewith. The discussion has ranged much wider and covered a very much broader field.
The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) read a section of a brief pertaining to a certain subject. I do not know who prepared it or whence it came but in any event it dealt with a much wider area than the motion does. Then the hon. member proceeded to make certain statements of fact with regard to particular things having been done in respect of this tax matter.
The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) said some things in his remarks about Pugwash park and so on with which I found myself in agreement, but the point I am seeking to make here, with deference, is that those remarks, however much we may agree with them, are irrelevant to the motion before the house.
Then, the former minister started to say what he had recommended in this particular case, and then he drew back from that and went on to deal with the larger question of the problems that arise in the double taxation field under the tax agreements between the two countries. This of course is a subject of great concern and very much open for discussion, but any discussion of it is not related to the particular case. I understood his remarks to indicate that that was what was involved in this case. Whether it is or is not, I find myself not in a position to say.
Here is the difficulty, as I see it. As a matter of public policy, surely the answer to this motion must be that since compliance with the motion would involve a disclosure with regard to the affairs of a particular person or a particular tax return, then surely we must adhere to the position that such information cannot be disclosed. In a moment I

am going to read the relevant sections of the act that seem to support that general doctrine. This doctrine has been asserted for years by succeeding governments in connection with all questions of this kind requesting information about particular returns-

I do not want to answer that question offhand. If the hon. member wants to deal with another question on behalf of the particular person who seems to have become the subject matter of this debate, although for the life of me I do not know why, if he wants to ask any questions of the other government, then that may be looked at. I would want to consider that rather carefully because that is quite a different thing from what is before us today.
In his remarks the hon. member made reference to sessional paper No. 189A dated March 12, 1959. I took the trouble to send to the Journal's office to get that return, but I find it does not in any way vary what I have just said. It does not violate, in any way, the position taken by myself as to giving the information asked for in this connection, nor the position stated by the former minister of national revenue on this same point. I do not want to read the return into the record because that would eat into the time available. However I invite hon. members to look at that return, and they will see it does not give any information relating to a particular tax return.
In support of the principle I have outlined, about its being contrary to public policy to give information about a particular return, I would draw the attention of hon. members to the succession duty act, which has since been repealed, but which governed the returns made in the earlier years in this particular case. Section 55 imposes an obligation of secrecy, and it reads as follows:
No person employed In the service of Her Majesty shall communicate or allow to be communicated to any person not legally entitled there-

to, any information obtained under the provisions of this act, or allow any such person to inspect or have access to any written statement furnished under the provisions of this act.
This was the provision contained in the old succession duty act. The provision in the Estates Tax Act is in slightly different form and says that, except as authorized by this section, no official or authorized person shall knowingly communicate or knowingly allow to be communicated to any person any information obtained for or on behalf of the minister for the purpose of this act. I merely cite these sections in support of the principle I have asserted.
It seems to me that the best case that could have been made from the remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur in putting forward this motion is that he is seeking papers in a particular case in order to make a general argument concerning Canadian-United States tax relations. I am sorry to have expressed it this way, but that is the best I can take out of his case. However desirable it may be, surely that general proposition cannot be used as an argument for disclosing the information in a particular case and to get the returns made in a particular case. It seems to me that is something nobody would question. Otherwise, any member in this House of Commons could come forward, and if he were skilled as the hon. member in making his argument on a general proposition that he wanted to discuss, obtain any tax return or any information on any tax return by relating it to a general proposition which is, properly the subject of the House of Commons. There is a method by which persons who are concerned with particular tax returns can get information, but it is very strict and very difficult and they must assume certain responsibilities when they obtain it in that way. Surely, they should not be able to come into the House of Commons and obtain not only the returns of taxpayers-

Perhaps I used the words loosely, but I have been accustomed to using them that way for many years. In estate work, you file the return on the prescribed form and it is invariably followed by a great deal of supplementary information by way of correspondence, company statements and other supplementary material. I have always used the term "tax return", when referring to that kind of correspondence, including all
Motions for Papers
the documentation because, except in very small estates, the information is rarely embodied in the first document filed.
In income tax cases that would not be true; but that is the practice in estate tax work, and I had used the income tax term rather in the sense of embracing all the information that is obtained in order to enable the tax authorities to make the assessment and to determine the amount of tax payable.
Now, there was one other assumption and I hope the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) will not mind my checking him on it. It was his assertion of his assumption of officials persecuting the taxpayers. In discussing a motion for the production of papers I definitely suggest it is going pretty far to make such assertions about what was done or not done in the particular case, because I am not in a position where I can come forward and agree or disagree. I am not going to agree with the figures he has given because that would be giving the information about the taxpayers returns by one device or another, and I do not propose to do that. I would hope it would not become the practice to make that kind of charge on these motions.
He referred to the generosity proposed by a former minister to Mr. Eaton. Surely that is not the basis of our handling of tax cases. To me it is absolutely essential that there be great strictness in applying the tax laws equally under the statutes, and I would hope there was nothing implied by any deviation from that policy, however worthy or unworthy the individual person concerned may be.
The point I want to make is that his worthiness or unworthiness is surely irrelevant, and reference to generosity of a taxpayer cannot be the basis of dealing with these matters. The obligation of a government must be to apply the taxes equally to all persons in precise accordance with the law, and I would take it that it was not intended to deviate from that.
I see it is getting on and my time has almost expired, but I would like to get a determination of this motion. For the reasons that I have given I have no alternative but to refuse the motion because I believe it means giving tax return information about an individual taxpayer's affairs.

Mr. Chairman, we heard before the supper adjournment a few innuendoes cast at members of the opposition for taking what I conceive to be a proper stand and being critical of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, particularly with regard to the composition of the commissions which must be set up. I noticed that when we were debating this question for a good portion of the afternoon the Prime Minister was in his seat. This to me indicates a proper interest in the amendment that was proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I am sure he was here to hear the remarks of hon. members in so far as they concerned the integrity of the leaders of the two main political parties in this country with respect to the appointment of members who would be comprising the commission that is to be set up.
I want to say a word or two about the comments of the hon. member for Port Arthur, when he was being so vehement about the integrity of the judges and the impartiality of the judges who would appoint the other two members of the committee. There were questions that we put to the hon. member which I do not think he answered satisfactorily and which I do not think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has yet answered in any satisfactory fashion. I am therefore going to put them again. Questions that occur to my mind are these. Here we have a member of the party to which the hon. member who proposed the amendment belongs saying that we should trust implicitly the judgment of the judges who are to appoint the other two members. They say this on the one hand, and yet on the other hand they say: We are not going to trust them absolutely, because we are going to subject them, in the third classification of these
23. 1964
Electoral Boundaries Commission selections which they may make, to the approval of the representation commissioner. It seems to me, sir, that you either have implicit confidence in the choice of the judges, or you do not have that implicit confidence. The very words of the third section of the amendment suggest that the member who proposed the amendment does not have that confidence which he says he has.
If you subject the selection of the judges to the approval of the representation commissioner, surely this erodes at the very foundation of the confidence of those members who support the member for Winnipeg North Centre in the amendment he proposes. It seems to me that if the hon. member asks the members of this committee to appear to be pure, he must also go the full circle and be pure himself. We have heard many words spoken in committee this afternoon about the lip service that is paid to impartiality and purity in the commission that is to deal with the selection of the members who are to serve on these commissions. I cannot think of any better provision than that which now appears in the bill to assure the impartiality that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre desires to be present in the commission which is to be considering the boundaries that are to be revised.
We have heard of the existence of certain maps. I have not seen any maps that have been drawn by the representation commissioner or his staff, but I think if such maps have been prepared we, as members who are vitally concerned with the composition of the commission, are entitled to see them; for surely if the representation commissioner and his staff have gone so far as to prepare these maps, I submit it suggests, sir, that a decision has already been made. I think the hon. member for Ontario raised a very important point. The point he raised was that the maps that have been prepared, have been prepared on the basis of a 20 per cent tolerance. If this is so, there surely has been a bypassing of the very responsibility that this committee is charged with, namely whether the tolerance is going to be 20 per cent; because if the maps as they exist have been prepared on the basis of a 20 per cent tolerance, it seems to suggest that the assumption has been made by those in power that this is going to be the tolerance regardless of the views of this committee and regardless of the views of parliament, and whether or not parliament passes this provision in the bill, the maps have been produced and these are to be presented to the representation commissioners.
This places the commission in the position of being a rubber stamp. This suggestion has been made before and it is one that has not

Electoral Boundaries Commission yet been answered by the Minister of Transport or by the member who has proposed the amendment. I say that because the general principle of the bill, which was adopted by the house, is that we should have some impartial method of revising the electoral boundaries. The more impartial we can be the more we will be keeping to the general principle of the bill.
The reason we are taking this step is that in the past we have been criticized for following the old method of redistribution. That method was to set up a parliamentary committee whose members were chosen, if you like, by the prime minister, the leader of the opposition and the leaders of the other parties. The present clause in the bill retains part of that principle. It is not quite as fair as the amendment because it retains the principle for only two political parties and not for the others. The amendment takes care of that, and I think that is all to the good. Either we want to get away from the old method of redistribution or we do not; and if we do not, let us be honest about it. But if we do want to get away from it and be as impartial as we can be, then I think the amendment offers a better way of doing it.

A study of this subject is really a study of the great members who have occupied either the treasury benches or the benches on this side of the house back to the time this country was founded. I am not surprised by the fact that a fair amount of emotion is attached to representation in parliament. I am also not surprised that some people here are making a genuine effort to be objective. I do not think that we should be ashamed that we wish to discuss a proposal which was first made in this parliament, as far as I am aware, in 1952 by a distinguished member of the treasury benches, the Hon. C. G. Power. I think I will cite Mr. Power because of the distinction he has brought to this house and the objectivity with which he has considered all aspects of redistribution.
In the 1952 volume of the House of Commons bills appears Bill No. 144, which was an act respecting the constitution and duties of the redistribution commission, a private member's bill by a very distinguished private member. Clause 3 of that bill might well have been adopted by the government, and if it had perhaps we would not be in the mess we are tonight. Clause 3 says:
For the purpose of preparing and reporting a plan for the division of the provinces of Canada into electoral districts in accordance with the provisions of section 51 of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1951, as enacted by the British North America Act, 1946, there shall be appointed a redistribution commission to consist of three members, one of whom shall be the surveyor general of Canada who shall be the chairman of the commission, another the person appointed on the recommendation of the Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons after consultation-
I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre might be interested in this phrase-
-with the various groups normally considered to be in opposition to the government at the date, and the third person to be recommended to counsel by the Leader of the party for the time being holding the majority in the House of Commons.
If I had no other reason for thinking that clause 6 was a good clause I would be persuaded by that extract from a bill presented by a man of the distinction of Hon. Mr. Power.

The second aspect I should like to discuss shortly is the matter of the appointment of judges. I should have thought that, long since, the Minister of Justice would have spoken to this point, and perhaps the bill would not have included the judiciary had he made the point clearly. I am going to cite Mr. Hackett, the former member for Stanstead, in a speech he made in 1947 as reported at page 5652 of Hansard. Mr. Hackett said:
I have understood from the prime minister that it is not the intention of the government to yield to the suggestion that has been made to it that redistribution be done over by what it pleases some to call an impartial body. That being the case, it is probably futile to discuss the constitution of any such body.
May I say that apparently it is futile to discuss the constitution of any such body because we are not getting much helpful assistance from the treasury benches. He continues: If that discussion ever becomes pertinent I shall place before the house my own reasons against the appointment of judges to such a commission. The right hon. gentleman who leads the house has indicated in no uncertain terms that he does not share my views as to the impropriety of appointing judges for the solution of quasi-political problems.
Surely this is a political problem and cannot be anything else but a political problem.
I think he must concede that the appointment of judges to draw an electoral map of Canada, especially where three of the judges would be of one political stripe and three of another, would be a great misfortune and a great folly. It would be dragging these gentlemen back into the dust of an arena which they had long since escaped, and it would be possibly a reason-a reason at least in the minds of some evil minded people- for appointing a man to the bench, that he might at some later time be used for a task of this description.
I will satisfy myself by saying that if such a proposal ever comes before the house and I happen to be a member I shall resist it, as I know all lawyers and judges will resist it, and as I believe everyone who thinks well of our legal institutions, especially of our judiciary, will be bound to resist it.
By the way, in 1952 much more time was taken than the three days we have been occupying. I have not gone through the debates on each redistribution, but this is a matter that occurs only once in ten years and I think that three or four days of debate on a matter of such fundamental importance automatically justifies the time devoted to it.
In my catalogue of greats I want to include Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, who in the 1952 debate on redistribution said that redistribution is not a matter of executive policy but a matter and a responsibility for the house as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we, on this side of the house, are surprised to see that the government intends to drop the legislation which was passed on March 23, 1962, with only one dissenting vote, that of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher).
I feel that such action on the part of the present government is undemocratic and constitutes an insult to parliament since at the time-the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pick-ersgill) will surely remember-all hon. members voted in favour of that legislation to promote the economic development of the Gaspe area.
I know that the government intends to spend $16 million to develop that district, especially seaports, but I do not think that will solve the problem and reactivate the economy of the area, since ships sail only five or six months a year while a railroad through the Gaspe peninsula would be essential for the development of mining claims.
At any rate, the president of East Sullivan gold mine, Mr. Pierre Beauchemin, holds a mining claim known as Federal Metals in the Gaspe peninsula, near Ste. Anne des Monts. He also has a prospecting licence valid in Gaspe peninsula's national park, which was granted to him by the provincial government following the decision taken by the Conservative government in Ottawa to build a railroad between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts.
This is very important, Mr. Speaker, and I ask the minister to tell us whether it is his intention to extend he period provided in the bill, because if he does not see to it, it will be the end of the whole project, since the bill expires on December 31, 1964.
That bill is important and essential to the development of the Gaspe economy, and the minister knows that, for nearly 30 years, his party promised to build a railway in the Gaspe peninsula. The Conservative government adopted a bill to make good that promise to promote the economic expansion not only of Gaspe but of Canada as a whole.
It must be remembered also that the province of Quebec has only 11 per cent of the railway lines in Canada, and that part of our country needs such a railway to develop its mineral wealth. The businessmen as well as

the chamber of commerce of the lower St. Lawrence region are desperate.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne), speaking before the Reform club in Montreal recently said that $7 million out of an amount of $16 million would be allocated for the construction of the Riviere du Loup wharf.
According to Le Soleil of last April 21, the chamber of commerce of north Gaspe did not like that statement made by the Secretary of State.
I would ask the minister to assure the people and the chamber of commerce of Gaspe that this bill, which has been accepted by all members, except the hon. member for Port Arthur, will be implemented. Even the minister, at the time, approved the bill.

When we came to office we examined the project and found there was no sound economic foundation for this railway. What was needed was improved transportation which would better serve the needs of the region. Let me point out that this parliament did not order the government to build the railway; it gave the governor in council permission to do so. We felt that before we spent $16 million of the taxpayers' money we should be satisfied it was being spent to the best possible advantage of the people of this region. We are engaged at the present time-it is no secret-in discussions with the government of the province of Quebec. There is a great need for the improvement of the highway from Mont Joli a little beyond Ste. Anne. REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CONSTITUENCY MAPS
speechtext:
Question No. 3 is the following:
Is the minister prepared to table any maps prepared by the representation commissioner under section 8 of the Representation Commissioners Act, for reference during the debate on the redistribution bill?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CONSTITUENCY MAPS
speechtext:
Section 8 of the Representation Commissioners Act which is to be found in the statutes of 1963 chapter 40, and which received royal assent on December 21, 1963, provided that the commissioner shall prepare maps showing the distribution of population in each province, and setting out proposals respecting the boundaries of the electoral districts in each province. I assume that the representation commissioner, with his usual dispatch, is proceeding with the preparation of those maps.
I have neither seen them nor inquired about them. However, I have heard rumours about them and the rumours I have heard are quite startling. I do not wish to go into those rumours but I think hon. members will understand that there is a good deal of concern about these basic proposals and the alternatives. I know that these are merely proposals, but I believe that the maps would give hon. members a fair idea of what is likely to result from the passage of the redistribution bill we have now been labouring with for so long.
I want to ask the Minister of Transport if he can now answer the question I raised this morning, and tell us whether in the opinion of the government these maps can be made available to the house. I cannot find anything in the act which says they are confidential, and there is at the present time no commission to which they can be submitted. Perhaps the minister could tell us whether it would require an order of the house for the production of these maps.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CONSTITUENCY MAPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be appropriate for the government as a government to express any view on this matter. The representation commissioner, like the Clerk of the house and the Auditor General, is an officer of parliament, not an officer of the government. Therefore I would not presume to make a decision myself on a matter of this kind.
That is precisely why I asked the hon. gentleman for time to answer the question. I wanted to consult the representation commissioner who, though he is an officer of the house, cannot respond for himself in the house. I have ascertained from him, since the question was asked this morning, that he has prepared or caused to be prepared by his staff-I do not think it is right to say he has prepared them himself because it is a technical job that he probably could not do-* sketch maps of all provinces, on the assumption that there would be a tolerance of 10 per cent. He has also had produced sketch maps on the assumption that there would be a tolerance of 20 per cent, and he is in the course of having prepared another set of sketch maps on the assumption that there would be a tolerance of 25 per cent. None of them is completed.
They are only sketches, and in his opinion the publication of them would be rather apt to create the impression, because we all know that people look at things and do not even read the big print, much less the fine print, that this was the finished product. It certainly is not, because the representation commissioner said to me that he himself could point

to dozens of objections in every one of these maps as they are now drawn.
He did make a suggestion which I am very happy to pass on to the house. He suggested that each party or group in the house might like to delegate three or four members to visit his office. I do not think we could reasonably expect him to be prepared to have every member of the house visit his office, because it would paralyse the work of the office and I do not think that would be right. However, he suggested that if three or four members selected by the caucus or by the leader would like to come and meet him and his staff and have the whole process explained fully to them he would be very happy indeed to do that.
I pass on that suggestion to the house as an eminently reasonable one. But I must say that personally I agree with the view he expressed that if these maps-as I have said there is more than one series of them-were published they would create an impression, which apparently has been created even in the minds of some sophisticated people like members of the house, that this is done when it is not done at all. All these sketches represent are exercises, as I called them earlier today, that were prescribed by parliament in the act that we passed unanimously at the last session.
